newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-U.K.Conservatives slam Labour spending plans.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-U.K.Conservatives slam Labour spending plans.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives, trailing badly in opinion polls ahead of a general election, reached on Wednesday for a trusted vote-winning formula and accused their Labour opponents of extravagant spending plans.
The party published a 100-page document which it claimed showed that Labour had already promised to increase government spending by 30 billion pounds ($50 billion) a year.

To pay for this, senior treasury minister William Waldegrave told a news conference, Labour would have to raise the standard rate of income tax by nine pence in the pound to 33 pence, and raise higher rates of tax to 70 pence in the pound.
The extra taxes would cost the average British family some 1,200 pounds over the next five years, he added.
"For all the rhetoric, New Labour remains the party of tax and spend," Waldegrave said.
Under economics spokesman Gordon Brown, Labour has rigorously avoided specific spending pledges. Brown repeated that any new spending by Labour would be matched by savings.

"The Conservative plan is to state a lie, repeat it, spend millions on advertising and posters to promote it, hoping that the bigger the lie and the more often it is repeated the more people will start to believe it," Brown told a news conference.

The narrow Conservative victory at the last general election in 1992 came after an onslaught by the party on Labour's spending plans which it then claimed would cost taxpayers 37 billion pounds ($62.18 billion) a year.
But the ruling party is in a much deeper electoral hole now than it was then, with opinion polls showing it some 20 points adrift of Labour and an election due by May 22.
With the parties sharply at odds over their spending plans, Waldegrave insisted the estimates his party produced were modest.
"The figures are, if anything, an underestimate of the true cost of Labour's promises," he said.

Prime Minister John Major said in an interview with the Press Association news agency: "We've only put in what is a copper-bottomed, clear-cut quote and promise, and we've added up what those amount to, and they do amount to an astonishing sum."

Labour, however, latched onto press reports that Sir Robin Butler, head of the civil service, had written to Major demanding it be made clear that he had played no personal part in drawing up their document.
"Sir Robin Butler has dissociated the civil service from the Tory political exercise," Brown said.
"His initiative makes it clear that their figures cannot be seen as objective, impartial, indisputable facts produced by civil servants but simply politically loaded costings."
